pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE and to bigger numbers and fractions: a child writes an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money problem, draws a bar model to represent and solve a fraction problem, and explains how a number-line diagram relates to the quantities in a situation (CCSS MP2). The number line is the pivotal new representation, and the IES fractions practice guide makes it central: it shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position, not two separate whole numbers stacked. This is where the load-bearing misconceptions live: children place 3/4 between 3 and 4 (treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), or count tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. Alongside, the operational equals-sign habit persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Good teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses unmarked number lines and bar models to force attention to the quantity, not the count of parts.
bestPractices: Use the number line as the central tool for fractions-as-numbers: partition 0–1 into equal parts, mark whole numbers as fractions too (e.g. 5/5), and contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits (IES Rec 2)
Use unmarked-between-endpoints number lines and 'what quantity is this?' questioning to prevent counting parts without understanding that numerator and denominator name a single number (IES caution)
Keep every number in an equation tied to its referent in the money/measurement story — units included — so translation stays meaningful (MP2)
Draw bar models to expose fraction and multi-step structure before computing (NCETM: reveals structure, precursor to algebra), then map the diagram to the equation
Translate in all directions among situation, bar/number line, and equation, explaining what each representation shows
keyRepresentations: Number line (fractions as lengths/positions; whole numbers labelled as fractions; equivalent fractions stacked above/below)
Bar/strip diagram for fractions and multi-step money/measurement problems
Part-whole and comparison bar models with an unknown
Symbolic equation with three-digit numbers and units tied to the story
commonMisconceptions: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, reading numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers
Counts tick marks or parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity
Partitions with the wrong number of marks (four hash marks for fourths) or treats the whole line as the unit
Keeps the operational equals-sign habit in multi-step money/measurement sentences and drops units off the numbers

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE, bigger (three-digit) numbers, money/measurement, and fractions. The core objective: move fluently among a real situation, a number line, a bar model, and a symbolic equation, explaining what each part represents and keeping every number tied to its referent (including units). The pivotal new representation is the number line, which shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position — not two whole numbers stacked. The load-bearing misconceptions: placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 (reading numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), and counting tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. The operational equals-sign habit (left-to-right compute; drop units) also persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses partitioning on number lines plus bar models to focus on quantity rather than count of parts.

activities.title: Place a fraction on a number line as a length
feedback: Target whether the fraction is placed as ONE magnitude, not whether a point was tapped: 'What single quantity is this point?'
If placed between 3 and 4: contrast directly — 'Locate 3, then 4, then find 3/4 between 0 and 1. Which is less than one whole?'
For partitioning: 'Dividing 0–1 into fourths needs three marks between 0 and 1 — how many marks did you use and why?'
When 5/4 is placed correctly: 'Good — a fraction can be more than one whole; say why the length passes 1.'
activities.rationale: The IES fractions guide makes the number line central for showing fractions as magnitudes and names the between-3-and-4 error as a documented whole-number misapplication; comparing the point's distance from 0 makes magnitude felt. An interactive placer with live length feedback and a whole-number/fraction toggle can make the mechanism concrete, but a fixed, well-drawn number line with the same partitioning task can also teach this — the interactive tool is proposed, not required.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Given a number line that runs 0 to 4, decide where 3/4 belongs before marking it.

If you first place it between 3 and 4, judge how far that point is from 0 — it stretches past 3, far too long for 'three quarters' (an interactive tool can light up this length, but you can equally read the distance on a fixed, accurately drawn line).
Drag or redraw 3/4 back between 0 and 1, partition that first unit into four equal parts, and mark three of those steps from 0.
State the single amount that point names in one sentence (e.g. 'three of four equal parts of one whole, which is less than 1').
Use a whole-number/fraction view to contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits.
Extend: place 5/4 and explain how a fraction can be more than 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is a single number with a magnitude — a length/position from 0 — not a numerator and a denominator parked side by side as two whole numbers.

activities.title: Partition an unmarked line and name the quantity
feedback: 'What ONE quantity is this point?' — answers that only recount marks have missed the goal.
If the wrong number of partitions appears (e.g. four hash marks for fourths): 'How many equal parts, and how many marks between 0 and 1 does that take?'
Praise answers that name the point as a single magnitude and justify the number of marks.
activities.rationale: The IES guide cautions that area/strip manipulatives can lead to counting parts without understanding, and suggests unmarked number lines with 'what quantity is this?' questioning; it also notes partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks. This activity focuses attention onto the named quantity rather than the count.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Start from a number line with only its endpoints (0 and 1) marked — no interior tick marks.
Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the number of equal parts needed for the fraction you want (e.g. four parts for fourths).
Say how many marks you had to add between 0 and 1 and why that many (fourths need three interior marks).
Point to the exact spot for the fraction and state what single amount that point represents — do not just count marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A point on the line names one quantity; the numerator and denominator together specify a single number, and partitioning into n equal parts needs n−1 interior marks.

activities.title: Build a bar model and equation for a money/measurement story, units attached
feedback: If the child grabs the visible numbers or computes left-to-right: 'Which quantity is the whole here? Map the bar before writing the equation.'
If units are dropped or mismatched: 'Put the unit back on each number and convert to one unit first — what does 3/4 of a metre measure in cm?' (3/4 m = 75 cm).
Check units match (metres vs centimetres) before combining — convert and name both quantities, so 245 cm and 3/4 m are expressed in the same unit, then subtract (170 cm).
Reward explanations that tie each symbol to the story and that identify whole vs part correctly.
activities.rationale: NCETM describes the bar model as revealing problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and bridging concrete to abstract; MP2 requires keeping symbols tied to referents and units, which here includes converting to a common unit before combining. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter document the entrenched operational view of '=' and recommend relational routines to remedy it.
sourceClaims: The bar model reveals problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and is a precursor to algebra; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

The operational view of '=' ('compute; the answer follows') is entrenched and persists with age; it interferes with writing structurally faithful equations, and is remedied by relational routines (true/false and open number sentences).
learnerActions: Read a measurement or money story, e.g. 'A ribbon is 245 cm long; 3/4 of a metre is cut off.'
Draw a bar model that shows the whole, the parts, and where the unknown sits.
Before combining any numbers, convert so every quantity is in the SAME unit — e.g. 3/4 of a metre = 75 cm — so you are not subtracting 3/4 from 245.

Write a matching equation in which each number keeps its referent and a unit, using the common unit you converted to (for this ribbon, every quantity in cm, e.g. 245 cm − 75 cm = ? cm; use £ or pence consistently when the story is about money).
Say aloud what each number in the equation points back to in the situation, then solve using the bar (245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm).
Translate in both directions: given an equation, describe the story and draw its bar; given a story, write the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations should be structurally faithful to the situation — each number carries a referent and unit, quantities must share a unit before combining, and '=' means 'the same amount as', not 'compute left to right'.

activities.title: Argue it out: where does 3/4 really live?
feedback: Never scored; push every answer to a because-clause with a reason about magnitude.
If the child guesses 'between 0 and 1' without partitioning: ask the follow-up — 'Show me the exact spot and how many equal parts.'
Accept a correction only when the child names 3/4 as a single quantity less than 1 and justifies the partition.
activities.rationale: Explaining how a number-line diagram relates to quantities is dialogic; presenting the documented misconception and asking the child to argue against it can check whether magnitude is genuinely understood rather than only recognised. MP2's emphasis on coherent, referent-tied representations supports mapping the proposed equation to the story.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (real or in-role) who places 3/4 between 3 and 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.'
Say whether you agree, then show and explain where 3/4 really belongs and how you found its exact spot.
Finish a because-clause: 'It goes between 0 and 1 because…'.
Judge a candidate equation the partner proposes for a money problem, and map each number to the story.
Tackle a follow-up — 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?', 'Where would 5/4 go?' — to defend your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining why 3/4 is not between 3 and 4 — and why the numerator/denominator pair names one magnitude — consolidates the concept and can expose shaky reasoning that a correct-looking placement might hide.

activities.title: Linked worked example: one story, four representations
feedback: Use as a worked example, not as evidence of mastery — follow with a construct-it-yourself task.
If the child relies on the highlighting to answer, remove it and ask them to produce the links from scratch.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal matched quadruple can illustrate correspondences but does not itself let the child place a fraction, partition a line, or respond to the magnitude misconception; it is a scaffold toward the construction tasks above, not a substitute for them.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.
learnerActions: Study a matched set: a story, its bar model, its number line, and its equation side by side.
Highlight (e.g. tap) one part and see the matching parts in the other representations light up.
For each representation, say what it shows that the others make less visible (magnitude on the line; whole/part structure on the bar; the exact relation in the equation).
Then, without the linked view, reconstruct the bar, line, and equation for a new story yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The four representations describe the same quantities; seeing the correspondences prepares the learner to construct and translate among them independently.

constraints: Reading/placing a correct point on a number line, or selecting a correct equation, is recognition; it does not by itself show the child can CONSTRUCT the translation or explain magnitude/structure. Pair any recognition warm-up (e.g. 'which point is 3/4?') with a construction-and-explanation task.

Illustrations and diagrams that are evocative rather than measured cannot be trusted for precise fraction positions; use tools or drawings where the partition is exact when the point itself is the learning target.

Unmarked number lines and 'what one quantity is this?' questioning are the intended scaffold against counting-without-understanding; if a line is pre-marked, the child may count ticks and bypass the concept.
Area/strip manipulatives remain useful but carry a known risk of children counting parts without seeing a single quantity — pair them with magnitude language and the number line.

Keep units on every number in money/measurement work and confirm units match (m vs cm), converting to a common unit BEFORE combining; the objective includes referent- and unit-faithful equations, not just a numeric answer.

The linked/tap-to-reveal worked example is a scaffold: it shows correspondences but does not require the child to place a fraction, partition a line, or confront the misconception, so it should lead into construction tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 'a ribbon 245 cm long, cut off 3/4 of a metre' mixes centimetres and metres; this is a genuine unit-conversion step (3/4 m = 75 cm; 245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm) kept deliberately as a referent/unit-tracking challenge. The conversion is now an explicit learner action and feedback item, not only a reviewer note, so a child cannot be left subtracting 3/4 from 245 directly.

The original 'the number line's refusal to lie' and 'the recompute makes fraction-as-magnitude felt' are motivational framing for a particular interactive tool; retained as an optional live-length mechanism, not asserted as the only way to teach magnitude.

Claims that fraction magnitude 'is not spatial-3D' and that a quiz 'cannot' show connecting representations were softened: recognition formats have an objective limit (they do not elicit independent construction), but no categorical medium-superiority claim is asserted.
Internal reteach-prerequisite references from the assessment field are left as source-internal data and are not surfaced as learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1? So which two whole numbers must it sit between? Show me why.'
'Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the right number of parts — how many marks do you need, and why that many?'
'Point to the exact spot for 3/4 and tell me what single amount that point is.'
'Where would 5/4 go — and does that show a fraction can be more than 1?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the between-3-and-4 placement, treating 3/4 as ONE number with a magnitude less than 1, and locating it by partitioning the unit from 0 to 1 into four equal parts and counting three — explaining that numerator and denominator together name a single quantity, not two whole numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers: places 3/4 between 3 and 4 because 'it has a 3 and a 4' — applies whole-number knowledge to a fraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a documented false belief — confront with contrasting cases (locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 between 0 and 1) and reteach placing unit and non-unit fractions on a number line as lengths from 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees with the between-3-and-4 placement, or locates fractions by their digits rather than by magnitude; may say 4/3 'isn't a number'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks/parts without seeing one quantity: gets a location by counting marks (or draws the wrong number of partitions) rather than treating the numerator/denominator pair as a single magnitude.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use an UNMARKED number line and ask 'what one quantity is this point?'; teach that dividing into 1/n needs n−1 marks between whole numbers and that the point names a single number (IES).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts marks to land somewhere, or partitions into the wrong number (four hash marks for fourths), and cannot say what single quantity the point represents.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign / number-grabbing in multi-step money/measurement sentences: writes a left-to-right compute or combines the numbers present without preserving the situation's structure or units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a bar model to fix which quantity is the whole and keep units on each number; reteach connecting the situation to the representation before symbolising.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a money/measure story the child produces a compute-then-answer equation, drops units, or grabs the visible numbers without mapping whole vs part.

responseLevels.gap: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4 (or by counting digits/marks); treats numerator and denominator as two whole numbers.
responseLevels.full: Places 3/4 between 0 and 1 by partitioning the unit into four equal lengths and counting three, explains numerator and denominator together name a single number, keeps referents and units when matching the equation — and transfers the magnitude reasoning to a new case (e.g. locating 5/4 beyond 1) unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 3/4 is less than 1 or belongs between 0 and 1, but locates it by counting marks or can't justify the partitioning — lists the steps without explaining the point as one magnitude; or handles the line but drops structure/units in the money equation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is putting fractions on a number line that goes from 0 to 4. They put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.' Do you agree with where they put it? Talk me through where 3/4 really belongs and how you know — and show me how you'd find its exact spot.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands fractions as numbers places 3/4 between 0 and 1 and can justify it by partitioning a unit into a length; a child applying whole-number thinking reads '3' and '4' as separate whole numbers and puts it between them — the two produce visibly different placements and different reasons. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'between 0 and 1' without the partitioning reason doesn't survive the follow-up, and a child who truly sees magnitude cannot place it between 3 and 4.
